drivers: Recovery balance not provided — missing HRV, sleep, resting HR, training readiness, and body battery data in input; ACWR cannot be calculated due to absent acute/chronic load metrics; however, aerobic decoupling remains stable (2.4–3.1% across recent runs), avg HR is steady (134–146 bpm), and no upward drift in resting HR or VO₂max decline observed

monthly_review.summary: September shows meaningful acceleration: faster pace, higher zone 3–4 time, and improved best effort pace vs August — but cadence dropped slightly and efficiency plateaued after prior gains.
monthly_review.highlight: Best pace improved sharply from 453 sec/km (7:33) in August to 369 sec/km (6:09) in September — a 84-sec/km jump that aligns with increased Z3–Z4 volume (52% of running time this month vs 34% last month) and suggests targeted neuromuscular adaptation.

goal_tracker.message: The runner has already exceeded last month’s distance (by +22.1 km) and sessions (by +4) with 3 days remaining — no additional running is needed to match August, and given the absence of recovery metrics, prioritising rest or very light activity over volume chasing is advisable.

insights.title: Zone 3–4 dominance correlates with pace acceleration but rising aerobic decoupling
insights.body: Z3+Z4 share jumped from 34% (Aug) to 52% (Sep), coinciding with best pace improving by 84 sec/km — yet average aerobic TE rose from 2.6% to 2.9%, suggesting early signs of fatigue accumulation within sustained efforts.

insights.title: Cadence drop (149 → 145 spm) accompanies efficiency decline (14.12 → 14.6 ml/kg/km)
insights.body: Lower cadence and higher oxygen cost occurred alongside increased Z3–Z4 load; notably, stride length increased (e.g., 86.49 cm on 2026-09-24) while ground contact remained stable (~305 ms), hinting at less economical force application under fatigue.

insights.title: Stable VO₂max (41–42) despite rising load suggests preserved aerobic capacity — but no HRV/sleep data limits confidence
insights.body: VO₂max held at 41–42 across 7 of last 10 runs — a positive sign — yet without HRV or resting HR trend data, we cannot determine whether this stability reflects true resilience or masked fatigue.

recommendations.reason: No recovery metrics are available to confirm readiness for further running stress; low-intensity non-impact activity supports circulation and parasympathetic engagement without load.

recommendations.action: Run 5.0 km easy on 2026-09-30 at pace > 8:30 min/km (510 sec/km) and HR ≤ 135 bpm — stop if aerobic TE exceeds 2.5% at 3 km.
